Exposure Triangle: Aperture: Aperture
The opening size controlling how much light reaches the sensor
f-stop
The number expressing aperture size, such as f/2.8 or f/16
Inverse relationship of f-numbers
A smaller f-number means a larger opening
Wide aperture
A large opening such as f/1.8 admitting substantial light
Narrow aperture
A small opening such as f/16 admitting little light
Depth of field
The range of distance that appears acceptably sharp
Shallow depth of field
A narrow zone of focus produced by a wide aperture
Deep depth of field
An extensive zone of focus produced by a narrow aperture
Bokeh
The aesthetic quality of out-of-focus areas
Subject isolation
Separating a subject from its background with shallow focus
Full stop of aperture
A change doubling or halving the light, such as f/4 to f/5.6
Fast lens
A lens with a very wide maximum aperture
Diffraction
Softening that occurs at extremely narrow apertures
Aperture priority mode
A setting where you choose aperture and the camera sets shutter speed
Exposure Triangle: Shutter Speed: Shutter speed
How long the sensor is exposed to light
Fast shutter speed
A brief exposure such as one two-thousandth of a second
Slow shutter speed
A long exposure such as one second or more
Freezing motion
Using a fast shutter to render a moving subject sharp
Motion blur
The streaking produced when a subject moves during exposure
Intentional motion blur
Using blur creatively to convey speed or flow
Camera shake
Blur from hand movement during a slow exposure
Reciprocal rule
Handholding at a shutter speed at least one over the focal length
Panning
Following a moving subject to keep it sharp against a blurred background
Long exposure
An extended shutter time used for light trails or smooth water
Bulb mode
A setting keeping the shutter open as long as the button is held
Image stabilization
Technology compensating for small camera movements
Shutter priority mode
A setting where you choose shutter speed and the camera sets aperture
Full stop of shutter speed
A change doubling or halving the exposure time

An image too dark, with lost shadow detail

Lighting Fundamentals: Natural light
Illumination from the sun or sky
Artificial light
Illumination from lamps, flash, or continuous sources
Quality of light
Whether light is hard or soft
Hard light
Light from a small source producing sharp-edged shadows
Soft light
Light from a large or diffused source producing gradual shadows
Diffuser
Material that spreads and softens a light source
Reflector
A surface bouncing light back to fill shadows
Direction of light
Where illumination comes from relative to the subject
Front lighting
Light from the camera position, flattening texture
Side lighting
Light from the side, revealing texture and form
Backlighting
Light from behind the subject, creating silhouettes or rim light
Rim light
A bright outline separating a subject from the background
Golden hour
The warm low-angle light shortly after sunrise or before sunset
Blue hour
The cool twilight period before sunrise or after sunset
Overcast light
Cloud cover acting as a giant natural diffuser
Color temperature
The warmth or coolness of a light source in kelvin
White balance
The setting neutralising a light source's colour cast
Fill flash
Using flash in daylight to lighten shadows
Three-point lighting
The key, fill, and back light arrangement
Portrait Photography: Portrait
A photograph focused on representing a person
Environmental portrait
A portrait including surroundings that reveal the subject
Headshot
A tightly framed portrait of the face and shoulders
Candid portrait
An unposed image capturing natural behaviour
Focal length for portraits
Around 85mm on full frame, which flatters facial proportions
Focusing on the eyes
The essential rule for a sharp compelling portrait
Catchlight
The reflection of a light source in the subject's eye
Rembrandt lighting
A triangle of light on the shadowed cheek
Butterfly lighting
Light directly above the camera creating a shadow under the nose
Split lighting
Light from the side leaving half the face in shadow
Loop lighting
A small nose shadow angled down and to one side
Posing
Directing a subject's position for a flattering natural result
Directing a subject
Giving clear friendly instructions to relax the person
Background separation
Using aperture or distance to keep the subject distinct
Model release
Written permission to use a person's likeness commercially
Group portrait challenges
Getting everyone's eyes open and everyone in focus

The focus point maximising apparent sharpness front to back
Enabling narrow apertures and low ISO in dim light
The three-layer structure that creates depth
Including a recognisable object to convey size
The warm directional light most landscape work depends on
A filter deepening skies and cutting reflections
A filter reducing light to allow long exposures in daylight
A filter darkening a bright sky while leaving land unchanged

Shooting several exposures to combine or choose from

Storms and fog often producing the most dramatic images
Visiting in advance to plan light and composition

The organised sequence from capture through final output

JPEG format

Importing
Transferring images from card to computer with a backup
Culling
Selecting the keepers and discarding the rest
Rating system
Stars or flags used to rank images during selection
Nondestructive editing
Adjustments stored separately from the original file
Global adjustment
A change applied to the entire image
Local adjustment
A change applied to a selected area
Exposure slider
The control adjusting overall image brightness
Highlights and shadows recovery
Restoring detail at the tonal extremes
Clarity and texture

Vibrance versus saturation

Cropping and straightening

Spot removal

Sharpening for output
Applying final sharpening appropriate to print or screen
Export settings

Backup strategy
Keeping copies in at least two separate locations
Metadata
Embedded data such as camera settings, date, and copyright

The span of greys between pure black and pure white
The separation between light and dark areas

The optical principle of projecting an image through a small opening

The first commercially successful photographic process, from 1839
Calotype
An early negative process allowing multiple prints
Wet plate collodion
A mid-nineteenth-century process requiring immediate development
George Eastman
The founder of Kodak, who made photography accessible to the public
Roll film
The innovation replacing individual plates and enabling handheld cameras
35mm format
The compact film standard that dominated the twentieth century
Photojournalism origins
Photography's adoption as a tool of news documentation
Dorothea Lange
The photographer who documented the Great Depression
Ansel Adams
The landscape photographer who developed the Zone System
Henri Cartier-Bresson
The photographer who articulated the decisive moment
Straight photography
An approach valuing unmanipulated sharp images
Pictorialism
An early movement imitating painting through soft manipulation
Digital revolution
The shift from film to sensors beginning in the 1990s
Smartphone photography
The change that made nearly everyone a photographer
Photography as art
The long argument over whether the medium qualifies as fine art
Portfolio and Critique: Photographic portfolio
A curated set of images demonstrating vision and skill
Series
A group of images unified by subject or approach
Sequencing
The order of images, which shapes how a portfolio reads
Editing down
Removing weaker images so the strongest carry the work
Consistency of style
A recognisable visual approach across a body of work
Artist statement for photography
A short text explaining intent and approach
Print presentation
Matting and mounting choices affecting how work is received
Online portfolio
A website presenting work to clients and audiences
Critique of a photograph
Structured evaluation of technique, composition, and impact
Technical critique
Assessing exposure, focus, and processing quality
Conceptual critique
Assessing whether the image communicates its intent
Receiving feedback
Hearing what viewers actually see rather than defending

Overvaluing images because of the effort behind them

Automatic ownership by the photographer at the moment of capture
Usage rights
The specific permissions granted when licensing an image

Documentary work requiring restraint that commercial work does not
